svg.title: Fig. 1 - Peak-centric versus spectral route
svg.desc: Panel (a): the peak-table route that this pipeline does not take - EIC extraction, chromatographic peak detection with area integration, peak table assembly and cross-sample alignment, drawn in grey. Panel (b): the spectral route. Each group contributes several raw files and one file is one sample. Scans of a sample are binned every minute; inside one bin every point is placed by m/z vertically and shaded by intensity; every point becomes one bar whose height is intensity, and bars below the intensity floor are dropped. Ions that recur across at least 50 percent of the files of a group form the candidate set; 80 percent is the bar for the comparison set. Every candidate is scored as intensity score times count score times relative-intensity score, the count score being deliberately inverted so that rarer ions score higher; the same three tables also score every ion of the run. Every ion is then checked for the heavy-isotope envelope: M+1, M+2 and M+3 are looked up at fixed mass offsets of 1.00335, 2.0067 and 3.01005 Da within the same minute, and only if the three successive abundance ratios fall inside the permitted window is the ion called an isotope of M and withheld from the differential list. Finally the 80 percent ion vectors of the two groups are laid on one shared RT and m/z grid: positions carried by both groups are shared ions ranked by their intensity ratio, positions carried by only one group are the differential ions, and the isotope flag travels with every row of the output table.
svg.text: height = intensity · dashed bars fall below the floor and are dropped
only ions that recur across files survive
candidates are the set that gets scored
total = intensity × count × relative intensity · the same three tables also score every ion of the run
count = how many of the 18 minute bins carry this m/z in one sample; inverted, so 1–2 bins score 10 and ≥10 bins score 1
M+1, M+2 and M+3 are searched at three fixed mass offsets in the same minute
a gated ion is a heavy isotope, not a new feature;
the flag is carried into every row of the table below
both group vectors on one RT & m/z grid; the table is written in both directions
paired when the minute matches and |Δm/z| ≤ 0.003
dashed tile = no ion there; B-only rows go to the mirror sheet
differential ion table · one row per 80% ion of A
count = files of the group carrying the ion
avg A/B = mean intensity ratio · 0 = partner missing
the call uses presence and abundance only; scores do not enter it
every ion keeps its m/z and its minute — no chromatographic peak is ever built
